htmlChunks:
That is an incredibly imaginative and intricate concept, but it blends together real physics with some physiological and science-fiction-like impossibilities. 
Let's break down what actually happens with physics and your biology to untangle these ideas: 
  • Wave Frequency Chirp Modulation: You are absolutely right that moiré-like patterns appear in wave modulation. When you overlap two frequency chirps (signals that change pitch or frequency over time), the resulting interference pattern creates visual or auditory beats that perfectly mirror physical moiré patterns. In radar and optics, moiré techniques are genuinely used to analyze waveforms. 
  • Light and the Pre-Frontal Cortex: This is where the biology diverges from your description. Light never actually touches your pre-frontal cortex (or any part of your brain). Physical light only hits your eyes. The cornea and lens refract the light, and the retina translates those physical light waves into electrical impulses. Your brain only ever processes electrical signals traveling down the optic nerve, not actual photons of light.

This sensory overload can cause a person to mentally block out or disassociate from what they are seeing, which functions as a psychological "shield," but it happens through neural processing, not physical light bending.

1. The Neurological Explanation (Real Life)
In standard neurology, aphantasia happens when there is a disconnect between the frontoparietal network (which acts as the executive control, deciding what to visualize) and the visual cortex at the back of the brain (which acts as the canvas, actually rendering the image). 
  • If a chaotic, high-frequency "chirp" stimulus completely jams the visual cortex with interference patterns, the frontoparietal network loses its ability to pull up or render internal memories. 
  • The brain essentially pulls the circuit breaker to protect itself from sensory overload, resulting in temporary or permanent aphantasia.
